analysis.one_liner: Lets employers refuse to hire paid union organizers who apply for jobs to organize workers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee in 2003 without ever getting a vote, despite 46 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the National Labor Relations Act to say employers cannot be forced to hire someone who applied for the job mainly to act as a union organizer or agent. This targets a practice called "salting," where unions send paid organizers to apply for jobs at nonunion companies so they can organize the workers from the inside. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially nonunion companies, gain the right to turn away job applicants they identify as paid union organizers, without that decision counting as an unfair labor practice. Union campaigns that rely on salting would become harder to run.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a provision to the National Labor Relations Act stating that nothing in the employer unfair-labor-practice prohibitions requires an employer to hire a person who sought the job in furtherance of other employment or agency status.
The bill's stated purpose is to relieve pressure on employers to hire people who seek jobs to disrupt the workplace or inflict economic harm designed to put the employer out of business.

analysis.who_pays: Union organizers and the workers they try to organize. Paid organizers could be lawfully rejected at the hiring stage, and workers at nonunion companies would lose one of the main tactics unions use to reach them, since the NLRB currently treats refusal to hire salts as discrimination based on union activity.

drawbacks.text: The provision reaches beyond paid organizers: it covers anyone seeking employment "in furtherance of other employment or agency status," and an employer could invoke it against any applicant it suspects of union sympathies, since current NLRB doctrine protects salts from hiring discrimination.

The employer-side objection it answers is real in some cases: unions have sometimes placed organizers in workplaces with the goal of generating costs for a targeted employer, which the bill's findings describe as inflicting economic harm to put nonunion competitors out of business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers get a targeted shield against a tactic they find coercive, but the cost falls on workers' ability to organize, because the same provision lets employers screen out union-backed applicants generally. Weighing who gains and who loses, the bill tilts clearly toward employers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: after referral to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee, no further action was ever taken and it died when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, with 15 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On July 21, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed.
The bill attracted 46 cosponsors (45 Republicans and 1 Democrat), but no committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Union organizers and workers at nonunion companies are better off, because the tactic of getting hired to organize coworkers remains protected under current labor law. Employers are worse off in that they still cannot lawfully refuse to hire someone because they are a paid union organizer.

for.name: Rep. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 15 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: House Republican cosponsors
for.role: 45 of the 46 cosponsors of the bill

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Boehner (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 11, 2003, and never reported the bill or scheduled a markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 21, 2003, and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 45 of the 46 cosponsors were House Republicans, with 1 Democrat, and there is no record of any Democratic champion for the bill.

industries.note: The bill would strip unions of salting, one of their main tools for organizing nonunion workplaces, by letting employers refuse to hire paid organizers. Workers' ability to join a union would shrink along with union reach, so union and worker interests run together here.

industries.industry: Nonunion employers (construction, manufacturing, and other union-targeted businesses)
industries.note: Employers would gain a legal basis to turn away union-backed applicants without committing an unfair labor practice. The benefit to them comes directly at the expense of workers' organizing rights, so their interest runs against ordinary people's on this bill.
